c.tagline: The world's salsa capital, where every night ends on the dance floor.

taxi.fareNote: Yellow taxis are metered, but many drivers quote a flat fare; agree on the price or ask for the meter (taxímetro) before setting off. Booking through an app avoids haggling.

emergency.note: 123 is Colombia's single nationwide emergency line connecting to police, ambulance, and fire.

avoid.reason: Elevated crime; avoid Aguablanca and eastern peripheries; caution downtown at night

hood_desc: Cali's premier dining-and-nightlife district, packed with the city's top restaurants, craft-cocktail lounges, and salsa clubs; compact, well-lit, and one of the safest bases for first-time visitors who want to walk to dinner and dancing.

The city's historic bohemian quarter of cobbled streets and colonial houses climbing a hill topped by a leafy park and chapel; full of cafés, artisan shops, salsa schools, and small boutique hotels, it suits younger travelers wanting culture and character.

An upscale riverside enclave between Granada and the center, home to some of Cali's most exclusive restaurants and hotels while staying quieter than Granada; a comfortable, refined base with nightlife a short walk away.

A modern, affluent residential neighborhood in the south known for green streets, gated communities, and shopping malls; the calmest, most family-friendly area, best for travelers who prioritize tranquility over being in the thick of things.

The dense historic downtown around Plaza de Cayzedo, the cathedral, and the Ermita church; rich in landmarks and street life by day but rundown and best avoided after dark, so most visitors sightsee here rather than sleep here.
lodging: Hotel Four Points by Sheraton Cali

water.note: Cali's tap water is treated and generally safe, though sensitive stomachs may prefer bottled.

transit.hours: MIO runs roughly 5:00am-11:00pm daily, with reduced late-evening and weekend frequency; there is no 24-hour service, so taxis and ride apps fill the overnight gap.
transit.note: The MIO BRT covers most of the city in dedicated lanes but can be crowded and confusing for newcomers; keep valuables secure and prefer app-based taxis at night.
transit.pay: Riders buy a rechargeable MIO smart card (around COP 3,000) at station kiosks and tap to enter; cash is not accepted at turnstiles. Cards top up at stations and authorized points. Each trip costs about COP 2,900.

bus: Intercity buses from Terminal de Transporte de Cali

transit.m: Airport shuttle bus to city center (45 min)
Official taxi to city center (35-45 min)

tip.r: Restaurants add a voluntary 10% service charge (propina) and will ask if you want to include it; adding or rounding up is customary but never obligatory.

food.name: Sancocho de Gallina Valluno
food.desc: Free-range hen simmered for hours with green plantain, yuca, corn and cilantro over a wood fire; Valle del Cauca's Sunday ritual with rice and avocado.

places.name: Ringlete
places.note: The reference for Valluno home cooking in Cali; brightly decorated and always busy.

places.name: El Zaguan de San Antonio
places.note: Traditional colonial-house restaurant in the old quarter doing classic Valle dishes.

places.name: Galeria Alameda fondas
places.note: Market kitchens serving huge sancocho lunches to locals at market prices.

food.name: Arroz Atollado
food.desc: Soupy Valle rice cooked with chicken, pork ribs, chorizo, potato and saffron-yellow colour, somewhere between risotto and stew.

places.name: Ringlete
places.note: Textbook atollado, generous and properly loose rather than dry.

places.name: El Zaguan de San Antonio
places.note: Regional menu with atollado, sancocho and Pacific fish dishes.

places.name: Galeria Alameda fondas
places.note: Cheap plates of atollado at lunchtime, straight from the pot.

food.name: Empanadas Vallunas
food.desc: Small corn-dough empanadas stained yellow with achiote, filled with potato and shredded beef or pork, fried crisp and eaten with aji.

places.name: Parque del Perro stalls
places.note: Nightly cluster of stalls selling empanadas, aborrajados and marranitas.

places.name: El Buen Alimento
places.note: Street-food classics done carefully, including reworked empanadas and arepas.

places.name: Galeria Alameda
places.note: Market fryers turning out empanadas all morning with fiery aji.

food.name: Aborrajados and Marranitas
food.desc: Ripe plantain wrapped around melting cheese and fried, and green-plantain balls stuffed with crackling pork; Valle's favourite snacks.

places.name: Parque del Perro stalls
places.note: The classic evening spot for plantain snacks with a cold drink.

places.name: Ringlete
places.note: Serves them as starters alongside the regional main courses.

places.name: Galeria Alameda
places.note: Fried plantain snacks made to order at market food counters.

food.name: Chontaduro
food.desc: Boiled peach-palm fruit from the Pacific coast, eaten warm with salt and honey; dense, buttery and reputed locally to be an aphrodisiac.

places.name: Galeria Alameda
places.note: Best selection of chontaduro, sold by weight and prepared on the spot.

places.name: Loma de la Cruz vendors
places.area: Loma de la Cruz craft market
places.note: Evening carts sell chontaduro with salt and honey beside the artisan stalls.

places.name: Bulevar del Rio carts
places.note: Street carts along the promenade, easy first taste while walking the centre.

food.name: Cholado
food.desc: Shaved ice piled with chopped tropical fruit, condensed milk, fruit syrups and a lump of lulo or blackberry; born in nearby Jamundi.

places.name: Loma de la Cruz stalls
places.note: Rows of cholado carts building the classic Valle version to order.

places.name: Parque del Perro stalls
places.note: Late-night cholado and raspao carts alongside the bars.

places.name: Jamundi cholado stands
places.note: The town that invented it, a short trip out for the original.

food.name: Lulada
food.desc: Crushed lulo pulp mashed with ice, lime and a little sugar - tart, pulpy and served in a tall glass; Cali's defining refresher.

places.name: Ringlete
places.note: Made properly with hand-crushed lulo rather than blended juice.

places.name: El Zaguan de San Antonio
places.note: Traditional drinks list including lulada and fresh fruit juices in water or milk.

places.name: Galeria Alameda juice stalls
places.note: Market juice counters make lulada and every Colombian fruit to order.

food.name: Champus
food.desc: Cloudy Valle drink of cooked maize, lulo, pineapple, panela, cinnamon and orange leaf, served ice cold and lightly fermented in flavour.

places.name: Loma de la Cruz vendors
places.note: Traditional champus sold by the glass beside the cholado carts.

places.name: Galeria Alameda
places.note: Market stalls keep tubs of champus cold through the day.

places.name: El Zaguan de San Antonio
places.note: Serves champus with meals, a rarity in sit-down restaurants.

landmarks: Cristo Rey
A towering hilltop Christ statue overlooking Cali, similar in spirit to Rio's icon, offering panoramic city views and a beloved pilgrimage and sunset photo spot.
La Ermita Church
A striking neo-Gothic church with slender spires rising along the Cali River, instantly recognizable as one of the city's most photographed architectural landmarks.
Cali Zoo
Ranked among Latin America's finest zoos, this lush riverside park showcases native Colombian wildlife amid tropical gardens, making it a favorite family destination.
El Gato del Río
A whimsical giant cat sculpture beside the Cali River kicked off an open-air art trail of colorful feline statues created by dozens of Colombian artists.
Cerro de las Tres Cruces
Three white crosses crown this hillside, a popular sunrise hiking spot where visitors climb for sweeping views over the salsa capital of the world.
La Tertulia Museum
Cali's premier modern art museum houses an impressive collection of Colombian and Latin American contemporary works within a striking brutalist-style building.
Plaza de Cayzedo
The historic central square, shaded by towering trees and anchored by a statue of independence hero Joaquín de Cayzedo, serves as the social heart of downtown Cali.
San Antonio Church and Hill
A whitewashed hilltop chapel surrounded by a bohemian, cobblestoned neighborhood of cafes and murals, offering some of the best sunset views in the city.
Boulevard del Río (San Antonio Riverwalk)
A scenic pedestrian promenade along the Cali River lined with sculptures and greenery, connecting the historic center to trendy cafes and salsa venues.
Parque del Perro
A trendy park in the San Fernando neighborhood, named for its dog statue, surrounded by lively restaurants and bars that capture Cali's nightlife energy.

train.note: Colombia has no intercity passenger rail serving Cali; travel between cities is by bus or air.

bus.note: Terminal de Transporte de Cali is one of Colombia's busiest, with 40+ operators. Frequent domestic services run south to Popayán (~2.5h) and north to Bogotá (~10-12h), Medellín (~8-9h) and Pasto/Ipiales, run by operators such as Expreso Bolivariano, Expreso Palmira, and Flota Magdalena.

ferry.note: Cali is inland with no passenger ferry service.

half.name: Lago Calima
half.blurb: Reservoir lake known for windsurfing and kitesurfing, ringed by pre-Columbian burial mounds and archaeological sites.

half.name: Guadalajara de Buga
half.blurb: Colonial city founded in the 16th century, home to the Basilica del Señor de los Milagros pilgrimage church.

half.name: El Queremal
half.blurb: Cloud-forest village on the Anchicayá River with natural swimming pools and waterfalls in the western Andes.

full.name: San Cipriano Natural Reserve
full.blurb: Jungle village reached only by motorized rail carts through the forest, with clear rivers for tubing and swimming.
